name: William Monter
specialization: Comparative French and Swiss witchcraft; regional variation in prosecution rates; legal and religious factors

major_works.title: Witchcraft in France and Switzerland: The Borderlands During the Reformation
major_works.significance: Key comparative study of two adjacent regions with markedly different prosecution rates, isolating legal and religious variables

major_works.title: Ritual, Myth and Magic in Early Modern Europe
major_works.significance: Broader contextual study extending witchcraft analysis within popular religion and magic

core_argument: Comparing adjacent regions with similar populations but different prosecution rates (France vs. Swiss cantons; Catholic vs. Reformed areas) allows isolation of the specific variables — legal procedure, religious culture, jurisdictional fragmentation — that drove or suppressed witch-hunting. Regional variation is the primary empirical fact requiring explanation.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Trial records from Franche-Comté, Geneva, the Vaud, and neighboring French and Swiss territories
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Prosecution rates by jurisdiction; legal procedures employed; confessional context of prosecutions
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Comparative regional analysis; quantitative prosecution data; legal-institutional comparative analysis
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Institutional-comparative: legal and religious institutions as primary variables explaining regional variation

key_contributions.claim: By comparing adjacent regions with different prosecutorial outcomes, historians can identify which institutional variables (legal procedure, confessional culture, jurisdictional structure) drove prosecution
key_contributions.implication: Comparative regional methodology is the most powerful tool for isolating causal factors

key_contributions.claim: Both Catholic and Reformed Protestant areas prosecuted witches, but different institutional structures and theological emphases produced different prosecution patterns
key_contributions.implication: Simple Catholicism/Protestantism contrast does not explain prosecutorial variation; institutional specifics matter

key_contributions.claim: Areas with multiple overlapping and competing jurisdictions (Imperial Germany, Swiss cantons) tended toward more intense prosecution as each court sought to demonstrate authority
key_contributions.implication: Political fragmentation was a structural enabler of prosecution cascades

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Comparative legal history; Reformation historiography; regional social history
criticisms: Borderlands focus may not represent broader European patterns
Comparative method requires comparable archival survival, which is uneven
Legal-institutional emphasis may underweight cultural and ideological factors

historiographical_significance: Monter's comparative borderlands study provided one of the clearest demonstrations of how institutional variables shaped prosecution outcomes. His methodological approach — hold cultural and demographic variables constant and compare legal institutions — influenced subsequent regional comparative work. His analysis of the French-Swiss borderlands remains a model of the regional monograph genre.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
